400.title: The youngest (1 Samuel 16)
400.hook: man sees the face, but the Lord beholdeth the heart; David is out with the sheep
400.carry: the lord looks at the heart
400.howItsDone: Catholics hear David's anointing at Mass, including on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle, and Catholic preaching turns to it when speaking of how God chooses the humble and overlooked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, the tallest man in Israel, hiding in the baggage on the day he was chosen. Your line was hiding in the baggage. Where did you step out? Day four hundred.

Four hundred days on this path, and today is a day about being overlooked. Saul's reign has gone wrong, and God sends old Samuel to Bethlehem with a horn of oil, to the house of a man named Jesse, Isai in the Douay-Rheims. One of Jesse's sons will be the next king. Jesse lines them up. The oldest walks in first, Eliab, and he looks the part: tall, strong, the kind of man you'd cast as a king. Samuel takes one look and thinks, surely this is the one. After all, the last king was chosen standing head and shoulders above the crowd.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL TO BETHLEHEM.` → `JESSE LINES UP HIS SONS.` → `SURELY THIS IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: And God stops him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Look not on his countenance, nor on the height of his stature." Then the line this whole chapter is built on: "man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart." Notice the dig at height. Yesterday the crowd cheered a king because he was tall. Today God says, don't measure that way. So the parade goes on. The second son, no. The third, no. Seven sons pass in front of Samuel, and to each one the answer is the same: the Lord hath not chosen this one. Samuel is puzzled. Are these all your sons? And Jesse says, almost as an afterthought: well, there's the youngest. He's out keeping the sheep. Nobody thought to call him in. A family gathering to meet a prophet, and the youngest boy is left in the fields with the animals. Samuel says: we won't sit down until he comes. They fetch him. And the text, honestly, says he was good-looking too, ruddy and handsome. God's choice isn't against beauty; it just isn't based on it. The Lord says: arise, anoint him, for this is he. Samuel pours the oil in the middle of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon David from that day on. The pattern keeps coming back in the Bible: the younger brother, the overlooked one, the shepherd. Catholics see it run all the way to Bethlehem again, where the son of David is born among shepherds, and to Mary's song: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble."
screen: `LOOK NOT ON HIS HEIGHT.` · `SEVEN SONS, AND NONE IS CHOSEN.` · `THE YOUNGEST, OUT WITH THE SHEEP.` · `ANOINTED AMONG HIS BROTHERS.` · then, large: `THE LORD BEHOLDETH THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone's heart today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a room you'll be in soon. A meeting, a family dinner, a class, the pew at Sunday Mass. Walk through it slowly in your mind, face by face, and look for the one out in the field: the person nobody thinks to call in. The quiet one. The new one. The one who always does the dishes. Stay with that face. What might they be carrying? What are they good at that nobody has asked about? If you pray, you can ask to see them the way the Lord sees, at the heart. The bell holds the time.
The youngest. David, Jesse's eighth son, left out in the fields with the sheep, and the one God chose because the Lord looks at the heart. Today's word.
Your line: the lord looks at the heart. Today, call in one person who usually gets left out, and listen to them. Day four hundred.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice saying about inner beauty.
what it means: right after Israel chose a king for his height, God tells Samuel not to measure that way, and picks the youngest, left out in the fields.
what a scholar hears: levav, heart, in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not just feeling. and the younger son chosen over the elder is a pattern across Genesis and beyond.

401.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
401.hook: a shepherd refuses the king's armor and faces a giant
401.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of David and Goliath in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholic schools and youth programs tell it as a story of trusting God and using the gifts you've been given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the youngest, called in from the sheep and anointed among his brothers. Your line was the lord looks at the heart. Whose heart did you look at? Day four hundred one.

Two armies face each other across a valley, one on each hillside, and for forty days nobody moves. Every morning and every evening, a champion walks out from the Philistine side and shouts across: send me one man. If he beats me, we'll serve you. Goliath of Gath. Huge, in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam. And every morning, Israel's army, King Saul included, stays put and is afraid. Then Jesse's youngest son shows up from Bethlehem with grain and loaves for his older brothers. He hears the shouting and asks: who is this, to defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `FORTY DAYS OF SHOUTING.` → `A BOY BRINGS BREAD TO HIS BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: David is brought to Saul and offers to fight. Saul says what anyone would: you're a boy, and he's been a warrior since his youth. David answers with his résumé: I keep my father's sheep. When a lion or a bear took a lamb, I went after it. The Lord who saved me from the lion will save me from this Philistine. So Saul says go, and does the generous, sensible thing. He dresses David in his own armor: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, the king's sword. David tries to walk in it. He clanks a few steps. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I cannot go thus, for I am not used to it." He takes it all off. Then the text slows down to show what he picks up instead: his staff, a sling, and "five smooth stones out of the brook," dropped into his shepherd's bag. Tools he knows. Goliath sees a young man with a stick and is insulted: am I a dog? David's answer is the center of the story: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts." One stone, slung, and the giant falls on his face. Two things are true here. The story is about trust: the battle is the Lord's, David says, not won by sword and spear. And it's about being yourself: David doesn't win by becoming a smaller copy of Saul. Saul's armor was a gift, kindly meant. It just wasn't his. He fought as a shepherd, with a shepherd's things, and that was enough.
screen: `YOU'RE ONLY A BOY.` · `THE KING'S ARMOR DOESN'T FIT.` · `A STAFF, A SLING, FIVE STONES.` · `IN THE NAME OF THE LORD OF HOSTS.` · then, large: `I CANNOT GO THUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use your own tools. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard in front of you this week, your own giant. Now notice whose armor you've been trying to wear for it. A boss's style. A parent's way of handling conflict. Someone online who seems to have it all figured out. Picture taking that armor off, piece by piece. Then look in your own bag. What are your five smooth stones? Patience, humor, a skill you practiced alone for years, a friend you trust. Name them. If you pray, you can bring your giant to God. The bell holds the time.
Goliath. The giant David faced with a shepherd's sling and stones from the brook, instead of the king's armor, in the name of the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: not in borrowed armor. Today, face one hard thing your own way, with the tools you already know. Day four hundred one.

what it means: a shepherd refuses the king's borrowed armor, fights with the tools he knows, and trusts that the battle is the Lord's.
what a scholar hears: the chapter states its own point in David's words before the stone flies: the battle is the Lord's, and he saves not with sword and spear.

402.title: David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18–20)
402.hook: a prince loves David as his own soul and warns him with arrows
402.howItsDone: Catholics hear part of the David and Jonathan story at weekday Mass early in Ordinary Time, in one year of the two-year cycle (1 Samuel 18–19).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goliath, and a shepherd who took off the king's armor. Your line was not in borrowed armor. What did you face your own way? Day four hundred two.

On paper, these two should be rivals. One is Jonathan, King Saul's son and heir, a brave soldier in his own right. The other is David, the shepherd who just killed Goliath, the new hero everyone is singing about. The women of Israel come out dancing after the battle with a song: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Saul hears it and something sours in him. From that day, the text says, he keeps a jealous eye on David. If anyone should feel threatened by David, it's Jonathan. He's the one who stands to lose a kingdom. Instead, something else happens.
screen: `A PRINCE AND A SHEPHERD.` → `HIS THOUSANDS, DAVID'S TEN THOUSANDS.` → `A KING GROWS JEALOUS.`

segments.voice: The friendship begins in a single sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit. The Hebrew verb means tied or bound together, the word for a knot. The two make a covenant, a solemn promise before God. And Jonathan seals it with a gesture that says more than words: he takes off his own robe and gives it to David, then his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt. The heir to the throne hands the shepherd the clothes of a prince. Then Saul's jealousy turns murderous. He throws a spear at David. He orders his servants to kill him. And Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He doesn't pretend the danger isn't real, and he doesn't abandon either of them. He speaks up for David to his father's face, and his father hurls a spear at him too. Then comes the plan with the arrows. David hides in a field. Jonathan goes out to practice archery with a boy. If he calls out, the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe. If he calls, the arrows are beyond you, David must run. Jonathan shoots. He calls out: the arrow is beyond thee. The boy runs off with the arrows, knowing nothing. Then the two friends meet, kiss, and weep together, David most of all. And they part with a promise: the Lord be between me and thee for ever. In the twelfth century, the English abbot Aelred of Rievaulx held these two up in his book on spiritual friendship: loyal when it costs a crown, honest when it's dangerous, and bound before God.
screen: `TWO SOULS KNIT TOGETHER.` · `A PRINCE GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.` · `CAUGHT BETWEEN FATHER AND FRIEND.` · `THE ARROW IS BEYOND THEE.` · then, large: `HE LOVED HIM AS HIS OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a loyal friend. Settle, and breathe. Think of a friend who stood by you when it cost them something. Someone who spoke up for you in a room you weren't in. Someone who warned you, or stayed when it would have been easier to go. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they did. Let yourself feel how much it mattered. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. Then decide on the words you'll use to thank them yourself. The bell holds the time.
nefesh. Hebrew for soul, the whole living self: Jonathan loved David as his own nefesh, bound by a covenant that cost him a crown. Today's word.
Your line: knit to his soul. Today, send one loyal friend a message that says exactly what they did, and thank them for it. Day four hundred two.

what a scholar hears: nefesh means the whole living self, not a ghost inside; 'as his own soul' is closer to 'as his own life'.

403.title: The cave (1 Samuel 24)
403.hook: David could kill Saul and cuts only his robe
403.howItsDone: Catholics hear David's mercy to Saul in the weekday Mass readings, and the Church reads it alongside Jesus's teaching to love one's enemies and not repay evil for evil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David and Jonathan's nefesh, and the arrow that flew beyond the boy. Your line was knit to his soul. Which loyal friend did you thank? Day four hundred three.

David is now a fugitive. King Saul has taken three thousand chosen men into the wild country near En-gedi, rocks so steep only wild goats climb them, to hunt him down. David and his men are hiding deep in a cave. And then, of all the caves in the desert, Saul walks into theirs. Alone. He's come in, the text says politely, to ease nature. He has no idea who is sitting a few yards behind him in the dark. David's men can hardly breathe. They lean in and whisper: this is it. This is the day the Lord promised. Your enemy, delivered into your hand.
screen: `THREE THOUSAND MEN HUNTING DAVID.` → `SAUL WALKS INTO THEIR CAVE.` → `THIS IS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: David creeps forward in the dark, close enough to strike. And he secretly cuts off the hem of Saul's robe. That's all. And then, the Douay-Rheims says, "David's heart struck him." Even that small cut bothers his conscience. He turns to his men and stops them from going any further. Saul is still, in David's words, the Lord's anointed. Saul gets up, walks out of the cave, and goes on his way, never knowing how close it was. Then David takes a real risk. He steps out after him and calls: My lord the king! Saul turns around. And David bows to the ground before the man trying to kill him, and holds up the piece of cloth. Look, he says, and he calls him my father. I had a thought to kill thee, "but my eye hath spared thee. For I said: I will not put out my hand against my lord." I will not. That's the whole story in three words. David has a reason, an opportunity, and men cheering him on. He also has the one thing that matters more: a line he won't cross. And for a moment, it breaks Saul open. "Is this thy voice, my son David?" Saul weeps out loud, and says: "Thou art more just than I." It doesn't last. Saul will hunt David again. Mercy doesn't always change the other person. But it changes who David is. Catholic readers see in this cave an early picture of what Jesus will ask: not repaying evil for evil, even when you could, even when everyone around you says you should.
screen: `SAUL ALONE IN DAVID'S CAVE.` · `ONLY THE HEM OF HIS ROBE.` · `DAVID'S HEART STRUCK HIM.` · `MY EYE HATH SPARED THEE.` · then, large: `THOU ART MORE JUST THAN I.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't take a chance to hurt someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has hurt you, and who, if you're honest, you could hurt back. A secret you know. A comment you could make. A forward button, a group chat, a review. Put yourself in the cave, the chance right in front of you, with everyone whispering: this is the day. Now let the chance go by. Say, quietly, David's three words: I will not. Notice how that feels in your body. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to keep that line. The bell holds the time.
The cave. Where David had his enemy alone in the dark, cut only the hem of his robe, and said I will not. Today's word.
Your line: I will not. Today, when a chance comes to get even, even a small one, let it pass. Day four hundred three.

what it means: David had every reason and every chance, and drew a line he wouldn't cross. his mercy moved Saul to tears, if only for a while.

404.title: Dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6)
404.hook: David dances with all his might and his wife despises him
404.howItsDone: In the Litany of Loreto, Catholics call on Mary as Ark of the Covenant, and the Vigil Mass of the Assumption reads the Chronicles account of David bringing the ark into Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave, and a hem cut from a king's robe instead of his life. Your line was I will not. What chance to get even did you let pass? Day four hundred four.

Saul is gone now, and David is king in Jerusalem. And he sets out to bring the ark of God into his city. The ark is the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, the place Israel knew as God's throne among them. The first attempt goes badly. The ark rides on a new cart, the oxen stumble, a man named Uzzah reaches out to steady it, and he dies on the spot. David is shaken. How shall the ark of the Lord come to me? he asks. He leaves it at the house of a man named Obed-edom, and it stays there three months.
screen: `DAVID WANTS THE ARK IN JERUSALEM.` → `THE OXEN STUMBLE.` → `HOW SHALL THE ARK COME TO ME?`

segments.voice: Then word comes that God has blessed Obed-edom's whole household because of the ark. So David tries again, this time with joy. After six steps he offers a sacrifice. Trumpets, shouting, the whole city out in the street. And the king, the Douay-Rheims says, "danced with all his might before the Lord." Not a dignified sway. Leaping, whirling, dressed only in a simple linen ephod, a priest's garment, not his royal robes. Up at a window, someone is watching. Michal, David's wife, Saul's daughter. And she "despised him in her heart." When he comes home she lets him have it: how glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself in front of the servant girls like some fool. David's answer is the heart of the story. It was before the Lord, he says, and "I will be little in my own eyes." He'll look foolish again if that's what praise costs. Catholics read this chapter with a second story beside it. In Luke's Gospel, Mary travels to the hill country of Judah to visit her cousin Elizabeth. Elizabeth cries out, why should the mother of my Lord come to me? It echoes David's question about the ark. The baby John leaps in Elizabeth's womb, the way David leapt before the ark. And Mary stays three months, just as the ark stayed three months in that house. Catholic tradition draws these threads together and calls Mary the Ark of the Covenant: the one who carried God's presence. You'll hear that title in the Litany of Loreto.
screen: `DANCING WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.` · `MICHAL DESPISED HIM IN HER HEART.` · `LITTLE IN MY OWN EYES.` · `MARY, THE ARK OF THE COVENANT.` · then, large: `DAVID DANCED WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise without self-consciousness. Settle, and breathe. Think of what holds you back from showing joy: in church, at a concert, at a game, in your own kitchen. The window where Michal is watching. Now picture something you're grateful for, really grateful, and let your body show it, just a little. Lift your hands. Smile with your whole face. Sway. Nobody's grading this. If you pray, you can offer that joy to God the way David did. If you don't, let yourself be glad without checking who's looking. The bell holds the time.
ark. The chest carrying God's presence, which David danced before with all his might, saying, I will be little in my own eyes. Today's word.
Your line: dance anyway. Today, show your joy about one thing out loud, even if someone at the window rolls their eyes. Day four hundred four.

405.title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 11–12)
405.hook: adultery, murder, and a prophet's story that makes the king see himself
405.carry: I have sinned against the Lord
405.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 51 (50 in the Douay numbering), the Miserere, at Morning Prayer on Fridays in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it to prepare for the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David dancing before the ark with all his might. Your line was dance anyway. Where did you let your joy show? Today, the same king at his lowest. Day four hundred five.

It's the turn of the year, the text says, the season when kings go out to war. David sends his army out and stays home. One afternoon he gets up from his bed, walks on the palace roof, and sees a woman bathing. He asks who she is. Bathsheba, Bethsabee in the Douay-Rheims, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers, away at the front. David sends for her. He's the king; nobody refuses the king. She becomes pregnant. To hide it, David brings Uriah home, but the loyal soldier won't sleep in comfort while his comrades are in tents. So David writes a letter, has Uriah carry it himself, and it says: put him at the front, and pull back.
screen: `THE KING STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.` → `A LETTER CARRIED BY ITS VICTIM.`

segments.voice: Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. Everything looks handled. Then God sends the prophet Nathan, and Nathan doesn't accuse. He tells a story. Two men in one city. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with nothing but one little ewe lamb, which, the Douay says, grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and "was unto him as a daughter." A traveler comes to visit the rich man, and the rich man doesn't take from his own flocks. He takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David is furious. The man who did this deserves to die! He'll pay it back four times over! And Nathan says four words: "Thou art the man." That's how the story works. David could see the injustice clearly as long as it was somebody else. The parable gets past his defenses, and then turns around. And David, who holds all the power in the room, doesn't kill the prophet. He doesn't spin it. He says, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers: the Lord hath taken away thy sin. The consequences still come; the chapters ahead are full of grief in David's house. But Nathan's word stands: the sin is taken away. Tradition gives this moment a song. The Douay's Psalm fifty, the Miserere, has a heading that sets it here, when Nathan came to David. It begins: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." The Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Catholics bring its spirit into confession: say it plainly, and hear the word of pardon.
screen: `NATHAN TELLS A STORY.` · `THE POOR MAN'S LITTLE EWE LAMB.` · `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · `THE MISERERE: HAVE MERCY ON ME.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a friend tell you a hard truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who could be your Nathan, the ones who'd tell you the truth to your face. Now ask what they might say if you gave them permission. Is there a pattern you can spot in others and not in yourself? Sit with the possibility without arguing. If you pray, you can say the first words of the Miserere: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy. Then think about who you'll ask, this week, to be honest with you. The bell holds the time.
Nathan. The prophet whose four words to King David turned a story about someone else into a mirror, and led the king to confess. Today's word.
Your line: I have sinned against the Lord. Today, when you feel outrage at someone else's wrong, ask once whether the story is also about you. Day four hundred five.

406.title: My son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33)
406.hook: the rebellious son dies and David wishes he had died instead
406.carry: would god I had died for thee
406.howItsDone: Catholics hear Absalom's rebellion and David's grief in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholics pray for divided families at Mass and in the rosary, some asking the intercession of Saint Monica, honored as a patron of parents with wayward children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's story of the little ewe lamb, and four words to a king. Your line was I have sinned against the Lord. Where did the story turn out to be about you? Day four hundred six, the end of week fifty-eight.

Nathan warned David that trouble would rise from inside his own house, and it does. Years of it. A terrible wrong between his children, a revenge killing, a son sent into exile, then brought home but kept at arm's length. That son is Absalom: handsome, charming, famous for his thick hair. He sits by the city gate and listens to people's complaints, and tells them, if only I were judge, you'd get justice. Slowly he wins the hearts of Israel. Then he declares himself king, and David has to flee Jerusalem on foot, weeping as he climbs the Mount of Olives. Father and son are now at war.
screen: `TROUBLE FROM INSIDE THE HOUSE.` → `ABSALOM AT THE CITY GATE.` → `DAVID FLEES JERUSALEM, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: The armies meet in a forest. Before the battle, David gives his commanders one order, in front of everyone, and the Douay-Rheims puts it tenderly: "Save me the boy Absalom." The boy. A grown man leading a rebellion to take his father's throne, and David still calls him the boy. The battle goes against Absalom. Riding a mule under a great oak, his head catches in the branches, the mule runs on, and he's left hanging between heaven and earth. David's commander Joab finds him and, against the king's order, kills him. Then the messengers run to David, who is waiting between the city gates. The first is vague. The second says it plainly: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David breaks. He climbs to the room above the gate, weeping, and says the words the whole story has been heading toward. My son Absalom, he cries, Absalom my son, and in the Douay-Rheims: "would to God that I might die for thee." Older English Bibles put it as would God I had died for thee. Count how many times he says my son. He has won the war and lost his child, and he would rather have died himself. Some Christian readers hear something more in that cry: a father who would die in place of a rebellious son. David could only wish it. For them, in Christ, God did it. And that's week fifty-eight: a shepherd chosen, a giant, a friend, a cave, a dance, a confession, and a father's grief.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a broken family. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a family that's split. Maybe yours. Maybe a friend's. A parent and a child who don't speak, siblings who stopped coming to the same table, a divorce that left someone in the middle. Don't try to solve it. Just hold them, the way David held Absalom's name even in the middle of a war. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for whoever has stopped calling whom. If you don't, simply wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
Absalom. The rebel son David still called the boy, and cried over, wishing he had died in his place. Today's word.
Your line: would god I had died for thee. Today, reach toward one person in your family you've been holding at arm's length, even with one small word. Day four hundred six.
